patient.history_present_illness: Mr. K. is a 54-year-old man with hereditary hemochromatosis cirrhosis (HFE C282Y homozygous, Child-Pugh B, MELD 16) and known grade II esophageal varices who was brought to the emergency department by his wife for progressive confusion over 6 hours and black tarry stools beginning yesterday. His wife reported that he had coffee-ground emesis twice at home approximately 4 hours before arrival, then became increasingly drowsy and confused. He could not recognize his wife at one point during transport. On arrival to the ED he was lethargic, could state only his name, and was intermittently agitated. He had not taken his lactulose or diuretics since yesterday morning. His wife confirmed he had not consumed alcohol for many months. He denied fever, chest pain, or prior head trauma. She noted his skin had a distinctive bronze-gray color that was longstanding, and that he had been followed every 6 months by hepatology with quarterly phlebotomy sessions prior to cirrhosis diagnosis. His last phlebotomy had been discontinued 8 months ago when ferritin fell below therapeutic targets, though he never returned to normal ferritin. His diabetes had been stable and his last HbA1c was 7.8%. He has no prior episodes of hepatic encephalopathy. The wife was concerned the confusion was entirely due to low blood pressure from the bleeding and that he would 'wake up once they gave him fluids.'

output.query: hepatic encephalopathy precipitated by variceal gastrointestinal hemorrhage management

results.title: Hepatic encephalopathy in chronic liver disease: 2014 Practice Guideline by AASLD and EASL
results.finding: Gastrointestinal bleeding is a recognized precipitant of hepatic encephalopathy in cirrhosis; the nitrogenous load from blood in the gut increases ammonia production. Treatment of the precipitating event (hemostasis, bowel decontamination with lactulose) is central to HE management. Ammonia level alone does not reliably grade HE severity; West Haven clinical criteria define grade.

results.title: Hepatic encephalopathy — definition, nomenclature, diagnosis, and quantification (West Haven and ISHEN)
results.finding: West Haven grade II is characterized by lethargy, gross disorientation, and asterixis. Grade III is somnolent but rousable with marked confusion. Both require active precipitant identification and management.

results.title: Review article: the modern management of hepatic encephalopathy
results.finding: Gastrointestinal hemorrhage contributes to HE through multiple mechanisms: gut bacterial metabolism of the nitrogenous blood load, hemodynamic compromise reducing hepatic ammonia clearance, and hypovolemia. Rifaximin and lactulose are first-line. Sedating agents including opioids and benzodiazepines should be avoided.

results.title: Hepatic encephalopathy
results.finding: In patients with cirrhosis presenting with altered mental status, GI bleeding is a common precipitant of overt HE. The combination of hypovolemia, increased gut nitrogen load, and impaired hepatic clearance creates a substrate for hyperammonemia. Diagnosis requires exclusion of structural CNS causes; CT or MRI is standard.

output.summary: Gastrointestinal hemorrhage is a well-established precipitant of overt hepatic encephalopathy in cirrhosis, mediated by gut bacterial catabolism of the intraluminal nitrogenous blood load, hemodynamic compromise, and reduced hepatic ammonia clearance. AASLD/EASL 2014 guidelines emphasize that HE grade is a clinical determination using West Haven criteria; ammonia levels are supportive only. Management requires simultaneous control of variceal hemorrhage, lactulose/rifaximin for HE, and active exclusion of concurrent precipitants (SBP, electrolyte disturbance). Ceftriaxone prophylaxis is recommended in bleeding cirrhotics regardless of SBP status. Benzodiazepines and sedating opioids are contraindicated.

interactions: Propranolol: should be held in setting of acute variceal hemorrhage and hemodynamic instability — beta-blockade blunts compensatory tachycardia and may worsen hypotensive shock
Insulin: hypoglycemia risk heightened in cirrhosis from impaired hepatic gluconeogenesis; monitor glucose closely during resuscitation
Spironolactone and furosemide: hold during active GI hemorrhage due to hypovolemia risk
contraindications: Benzodiazepines — CNS depressants that precipitate and deepen hepatic encephalopathy; contraindicated for agitation management in HE
Sedating opioids (morphine, hydromorphone) — hepatic metabolism impaired in cirrhosis; accumulate and worsen HE
NSAIDs — risk of renal vasoconstriction and hepatorenal syndrome in hypovolemic cirrhotic; contraindicated

Ceftriaxone: standard SBP prophylaxis in bleeding cirrhotics regardless of paracentesis result; no hepatotoxic concern at standard doses
Lactulose: may be administered by enema if patient unable to take orally; monitor for electrolyte disturbance with frequent stooling
Rifaximin: minimally absorbed; safe in hepatic dysfunction

For pain: acetaminophen 500-1000 mg with dose reduction in severe hepatic dysfunction preferred over opioids or NSAIDs

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Hepatic encephalopathy (West Haven grade II-III), hereditary hemochromatosis cirrhosis, precipitated by acute variceal hemorrhage (upper GI bleed with melena and coffee-ground emesis)

differential.key_features: BP 96/60, HR 118, Hgb 7.2 — shock is present and contributes to cerebral hypoperfusion, but elevated ammonia 112 µmol/L and cirrhosis indicate HE is a co-primary mechanism not explainable by hemodynamics alone.

BUN 58 with BUN:Cr ratio 44.6 (markedly elevated) — ratio is pre-renal/GI-blood-load in pattern; true uremic encephalopathy requires sustained renal failure with BUN typically >100 and GFR <15; creatinine only 1.3.
INR 2.0, platelets 72 — coagulopathy elevates hemorrhagic stroke risk; non-contrast CT head excludes intracranial hemorrhage.
Ascites present; SBP must be excluded by paracentesis; ascitic PMN 74 — SBP not confirmed on follow-up.
Insulin-dependent diabetic with impaired hepatic gluconeogenesis; blood glucose 148 on admission — hypoglycemia excluded at presentation.
No heavy alcohol use history; no ophthalmoplegia or nystagmus; hemochromatosis cirrhosis without classic malnutrition risk — empiric thiamine is still prudent before glucose-containing fluids.

useless_tools.rationale: No clinical suspicion for hepatopulmonary syndrome, portopulmonary hypertension, or endocarditis; echocardiography is not part of the HE or acute variceal bleed workup.
Amyloid PET has no role in HE workup; reversible metabolic encephalopathy is the diagnosis under consideration.
DaTscan has no role in HE workup; the question is metabolic encephalopathy, not nigrostriatal degeneration.

sequence_constraints.reason: In altered mental status with coagulopathy and thrombocytopenia, exclude intracranial hemorrhage and mass effect on CT before any LP to avoid herniation risk.

critical_actions: Resuscitate with IV crystalloid and packed red blood cells (target Hgb 7-8 g/dL; restrictive transfusion to reduce rebleeding risk from portal hypertension).
Hold propranolol immediately — beta-blockade is contraindicated in acute hemodynamic decompensation from variceal hemorrhage.
Start octreotide 50 mcg IV bolus then 50 mcg/hr infusion (or terlipressin if available) to reduce portal pressure and slow variceal hemorrhage.
Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily — standard antibiotic prophylaxis in bleeding cirrhotics regardless of SBP paracentesis result, per AASLD/EASL.
Lactulose via nasogastric tube or rectal enema (patient unable to take orally) titrated to 2-4 soft stools per day; add rifaximin 550 mg via NG tube.
Empiric IV thiamine 100 mg before any dextrose-containing fluids.
Urgent upper endoscopy for diagnosis and hemostasis (variceal band ligation or sclerotherapy) once hemodynamically stabilized.
Non-contrast CT head to exclude intracranial hemorrhage given coagulopathy (INR 2.0) and thrombocytopenia (platelets 72) before any LP.
Diagnostic paracentesis to exclude SBP as concurrent HE precipitant.
Hold spironolactone and furosemide during active hemorrhage and hemodynamic instability.
contraindicated_actions: Do not administer benzodiazepines for agitation — they precipitate and deepen HE in cirrhotic patients; use haloperidol (lowest effective dose) for acute agitation.
Do not use sedating opioids — hepatic clearance is impaired in cirrhosis; they accumulate and worsen HE.

Do not attribute the altered mental status solely to hemorrhagic shock and expect full resolution with fluid resuscitation alone — ammonia 112 µmol/L and cirrhosis indicate active HE requiring specific treatment.

Do not attribute the markedly elevated BUN:Cr ratio (44.6) solely to intrinsic renal failure or uremia — the ratio pattern is consistent with upper GI nitrogen load from digested blood, not primary uremic encephalopathy.
Do not transfuse to normalization of hemoglobin — overtransfusion increases portal pressure and rebleeding risk in variceal hemorrhage.
Do not perform LP before non-contrast CT head excludes intracranial hemorrhage given coagulopathy.
key_reasoning_points: Gastrointestinal blood acts as a high-protein nitrogenous load in the gut; bacterial catabolism produces ammonia that overwhelms an already-impaired hepatic clearance mechanism, directly precipitating HE — the bleed is both the cause of hemodynamic compromise AND the source of excess ammonia.

The markedly elevated BUN:Cr ratio (44.6) reflects intraluminal blood digestion (upper GI bleed), not primary intrinsic renal failure; a naive agent anchoring on the elevated BUN may misattribute AMS to uremic encephalopathy and undertreat the HE.

Hemodynamic shock contributes to AMS through cerebral hypoperfusion, but the co-occurrence of ammonia elevation, cirrhosis, asterixis, and West Haven grade II-III features in a patient with known varices and a GI bleed points to HE as the primary neurological mechanism — both must be treated simultaneously.

Hereditary hemochromatosis cirrhosis carries the same portal hypertension physiology as other etiologies of cirrhosis; the elevated ferritin/transferrin saturation contextualizes the underlying liver disease but the diagnosis and management of HE and variceal hemorrhage follow standard protocols.

Coagulopathy (INR 2.0) and thrombocytopenia (platelets 72) substantially raise the risk of intracranial hemorrhage — a non-contrast CT head is mandatory before LP and is especially urgent when the diagnosis of HE might be challenged by a competing structural cause.

Propranolol is the long-term mainstay of variceal hemorrhage prophylaxis but must be held acutely when the patient is hypotensive and tachycardic — its beta-blockade prevents the compensatory tachycardia needed to maintain cardiac output during active hemorrhage.

red_herrings.intended_effect: Interpret the disproportionately elevated BUN as evidence of uremic encephalopathy and attribute AMS primarily to renal failure rather than HE precipitated by the GI bleed.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: BUN:Cr ratio >20 in the setting of an upper GI bleed reflects intraluminal blood digestion and gut absorption of urea nitrogen — a pre-renal/GI-nitrogen-load pattern, not primary renal failure. Creatinine 1.3 is only mildly elevated. True uremic encephalopathy requires sustained high BUN (typically >100) with severe renal failure; this pattern is the GI bleed nitrogen load precipitating HE, not uremia.

red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute AMS entirely to hemorrhagic/hypovolemic shock and cerebral hypoperfusion, expecting mental status to normalize with fluid resuscitation alone without specific HE treatment.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Hemodynamic shock contributes to altered mental status but cannot explain the full picture: ammonia 112 µmol/L, established cirrhosis, asterixis, and West Haven grade II-III features indicate active HE requiring lactulose, rifaximin, and precipitant control beyond resuscitation alone.
